The cluster-level geometric mean prevalence of CMD, defined as an SSQ score of ≥8, was 19.4% when ACASI was used and 14.1% when using SAQ ( Table 2 ), and there was weak evidence of an association of CMD with the ACASI trial arm [risk ratio (RR) 1.37, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.99, 1.89; P = .056].

There was no evidence of a difference between arms in the proportion of all participants who received counselling [cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 13.2% vs 12.1%, adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 1.09, 95% CI 0.70–1.71; P = .71].
49.Rationale: The passage provides direct evidence that ACASI elicited higher prevalences of reported IPV and higher CMD scores (geometric mean prevalence and continuous SSQ increase), indicating more potential cases were identified with ACASI. It also explicitly reports no evidence of a difference between arms in the proportion of participants who received counselling. The option faithfully summarizes these findings and is therefore derivable from the passage.

49.Option: The observed increase in the prevalence of CMD and IPV when using ACASI could have been due to an increase in the false-positive rate rather than a decrease in the false-negative rate.
Evidence: Less evidence is available for the effectiveness of ACASI for other sensitive topics such as experience of abuse [ 4 ] or symptoms of mental health disorders, particularly in low-income settings.
ACASI data collection was associated with increased reporting of all forms of IPV (cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 41.1% compared with 20.8%, RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.55, 2.57; P < .001).

The cluster-level geometric mean prevalence of CMD, defined as an SSQ score of ≥8, was 19.4% when ACASI was used and 14.1% when using SAQ ( Table 2 ), and there was weak evidence of an association of CMD with the ACASI trial arm [risk ratio (RR) 1.37, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.99, 1.89; P = .056].
49.Rationale: The passage shows increased reporting with ACASI but does not provide any validation against a gold standard to distinguish true positives from false positives. While it is theoretically possible that increased prevalence reflects more false positives rather than fewer false negatives, that alternative explanation is speculative and not supported or evaluated in the text. The passage notes limited evidence about ACASI's effectiveness for these topics in low-income settings, but it does not provide data to attribute the observed increases specifically to higher false-positive rates. Therefore the specific causal conjecture in the option cannot be derived from the passage.

49.Option: The higher reporting of IPV in men using ACASI may reflect greater willingness among men to disclose abuse due to the perceived anonymity of the digital tool, which aligns with traditional masculine norms of emotional restraint.
Evidence: ACASI was associated with increased prevalence of reports of all forms of IPV in both men and women ( Table 4 ) with no evidence of interaction by gender ( t = 0.15, P = .88).

In men, the geometric mean prevalences of both outcomes were very different from the overall prevalences by arm because the number of men per workday was often small (mean cluster size 4.4) and many clusters had no cases. Only 59 clusters had any men who completed the IPV questions and in only 38 did any men report IPV.
ACASI is thought to remove social pressure and give a sense of privacy [ 4 ].
49.Rationale: While the passage reports increased IPV reporting with ACASI in both sexes and notes that ACASI may reduce social pressure and afford privacy, it does not provide evidence that the higher reporting in men is due to greater willingness to disclose driven by perceived anonymity. Moreover, the passage explicitly cautions that male sample sizes were small and many clusters had no male cases, undermining robustness of any male-specific inference. The claim that this aligns with traditional masculine norms of emotional restraint is an external cultural explanation not presented or supported in the text. Thus the specific interpretation in the option cannot be inferred from the passage.

49.Option: The feasibility and acceptability of ACASI in low-income settings are well established, as demonstrated by high participant engagement and low technical failure rates during the trial.
Evidence: Less evidence is available for the effectiveness of ACASI for other sensitive topics such as experience of abuse [ 4 ] or symptoms of mental health disorders, particularly in low-income settings.
The trial enrolled from 20 February to 10 June 2022, encompassing 71 team workdays (clusters) and 1240 participants ( Supplementary Table S1 ).
Questions and possible responses were recorded in English, Shona, and Ndebele by female research assistants. Participants chose their language of preference.
49.Rationale: The passage does not state that feasibility and acceptability of ACASI in low-income settings are "well established." In fact, it explicitly notes that there is less evidence about ACASI's effectiveness for some sensitive topics in low-income settings. Although the trial successfully enrolled participants using ACASI, the paper does not provide metrics of participant engagement or technical failure rates and does not claim general establishment of feasibility/acceptability. Therefore the strong conclusion in the option is not supported by the passage.

50.Option: The validity of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness studies conducted at the primary care level may be jeopardized if vaccination status influences self-testing behavior and self-test results influence GP consultation, particularly when these effects occur in opposite directions.
Evidence: COVID-19 vaccination status may impact self-testing behaviours, e.g. if vaccinated persons are more likely to self-test [ 11 ], and knowing the self-test result may affect GP consultation behaviour.
This effect may occur through a person testing negative being more likely to consult the GP, or a person testing positive being more likely to consult the GP.
In the context of a TND study, the combination of these two effects could introduce bias (see a numerical example in Supplementary Tables S1–S3 ).

The most extreme bias of 45% occurred with a 20% VE, 30% self-testing among the unvaccinated and 2.5 times higher self-testing among the vaccinated, and the largest difference between GP consultation behaviours after a positive or negative self-test result (i.e. consultation probability ratio of 2 after a positive self-test, combined with consultation probability ratio of 0.5 after a negative self-test, or vice versa) ( Supplementary Fig. S2 and Table S4 ).
With equal probability ratios of consultation after negative and positive self-tests, VE was not biased.
50.Rationale: The passage explicitly states vaccination may affect self-testing and that knowledge of self-test results may alter GP consultation. It further states that the combination of these effects can introduce bias in TND VE estimates and shows via simulation that bias is largest when consultation probabilities after positive and negative self-tests differ (opposite directions). Therefore the concern that VE validity may be jeopardized under those conditions is directly supported.

50.Option: The primary care test-negative design is inherently invalid in settings where self-testing is prevalent, regardless of vaccination status or consultation behavior.
Evidence: This bias in COVID-19 VE can be mitigated by adjusting the logistic regression model by self-test use (yes/no), if this information is collected within the study without misclassification.
While a selection bias is introduced into the study, it can be mitigated with techniques used to adjust for confounding, such as regression modelling [ 20 , 21 ].
In Fig. 1, there are no non-causal paths open between COVID-19 vaccination and SARS-CoV-2 infection. The causal odds ratio, and hereafter unbiased VE, may thus be estimated.
50.Rationale: The passage does not claim inherent invalidity of the TND when self-testing is prevalent. Instead it describes a potential bias mechanism but explicitly shows this bias can be mitigated by collecting self-test use and adjusting for it in analysis. It also states that in the absence of self-tests the causal VE can be unbiased. Therefore the absolute statement of inherent invalidity is not supported.

50.Option: The most extreme bias in vaccine effectiveness estimates occurs when vaccinated individuals are less likely to self-test and more likely to consult the GP after a negative result.
Evidence: The most extreme bias of 45% occurred with a 20% VE, 30% self-testing among the unvaccinated and 2.5 times higher self-testing among the vaccinated, and the largest difference between GP consultation behaviours after a positive or negative self-test result (i.e. consultation probability ratio of 2 after a positive self-test, combined with consultation probability ratio of 0.5 after a negative self-test, or vice versa) ( Supplementary Fig. S2 and Table S4 ).
COVID-19 vaccination status may impact self-testing behaviours, e.g. if vaccinated persons are more likely to self-test [ 11 ]
50.Rationale: The passage's simulation indicates the most extreme bias occurred when vaccinated persons were more likely to self-test (not less likely) combined with large differences in GP consultation after positive vs negative self-tests. Option 2 describes the opposite situation and is not supported by the evidence presented.

50.Option: The use of self-tests in the general population may reduce the overall burden on primary care systems by decreasing unnecessary GP consultations for individuals who test negative.
Evidence: knowing the self-test result may affect GP consultation behaviour.
This effect may occur through a person testing negative being more likely to consult the GP, or a person testing positive being more likely to consult the GP.
50.Rationale: The passage states that self-test results can either increase or decrease GP consultation depending on the context (a negative result could make someone more or less likely to consult, likewise for a positive result). It does not claim or provide evidence that self-testing reduces primary care burden overall. Thus the inference that self-tests will decrease unnecessary GP consultations and reduce burden is not supported by the passage.

50.Option: Self-testing behavior is primarily driven by healthcare-seeking behavior, which is already controlled for in test-negative design studies, minimizing the risk of bias.
Evidence: healthcare-seeking behaviour, defined as one’s propensity to seek care, is a determinant of vaccination, GP consultation, and self-testing [ 7 ].
In TND studies, it is generally assumed that healthcare-seeking behaviour is (at least partially) controlled for by design [ 7 ].
This study focuses on bias emerging from an effect of vaccination on self-testing that is independent from healthcare-seeking behaviour.
50.Rationale: Although healthcare-seeking behaviour influences self-testing, the authors explicitly focus on bias arising from vaccination affecting self-testing independently of healthcare-seeking. Thus self-testing is not portrayed as being driven solely by healthcare-seeking and the potential for bias remains even when healthcare-seeking is controlled for in the TND. Therefore the statement that risk of bias is minimized for this reason is unsupported.

51.Option: The use of probabilistic trend categorization—such as stable, increase, or decrease—enhances the utility of forecasts for decision-making by providing interpretable, actionable insights into future epidemic trajectories.
Evidence: Lastly, the use of prediction samples allows us to assign probabilities to different interpretable trend categories (stable, increase, and decrease) by using thresholds agreed with disease and operations experts at all geographies.
This provides enough foresight to be useful, with meaningfully small uncertainty, agreed with end users of the forecasts.
51.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that prediction samples are used to assign probabilities to interpretable trend categories (stable/increase/decrease) and that these choices are agreed with disease and operations experts and end users. From an epidemiological perspective, providing probabilistic, interpretable trend categories converts raw forecasts into actionable information for decision-makers, so the inference that this enhances utility for decision-making is directly supported by the quoted text.

51.Option: The probabilistic trend categorization enables modelers to identify and exclude underperforming models during weekly quality checks, improving forecast reliability.
Evidence: Lastly, the use of prediction samples allows us to assign probabilities to different interpretable trend categories (stable, increase, and decrease) by using thresholds agreed with disease and operations experts at all geographies.
Each week, models are first inspected by the team (applying expert judgment) and then candidate models are ensembled.
While quantitative scoring is a key component in developing our ensemble, within-team expert judgment is necessary to exclude models weekly.
51.Rationale: The passage describes two separate practices: (a) assigning probabilistic trend categories from prediction samples, and (b) weekly inspection and exclusion of models using expert judgment and quantitative scoring. It does not state that the probabilistic trend categorization is the basis for identifying or excluding underperforming models. Therefore the specific causal claim that the trend categorization enables model exclusion during weekly checks is not supported by the passage.

51.Option: The use of a 14-day forecast horizon provides sufficient foresight for stakeholders to plan long-term healthcare infrastructure investments and staffing strategies.
Evidence: As a trade-off between long forecast horizons with high uncertainty and short horizons with lower utility, we chose a consistent 14-day horizon across all models. This provides enough foresight to be useful, with meaningfully small uncertainty, agreed with end users of the forecasts.

Public health and healthcare leaders better use scarce resources when they can predict hospital admissions and bed occupancy, reallocating staff and beds to elective care as emergency admissions decline.
51.Rationale: The passage states that a 14-day horizon was chosen to provide useful short-term foresight with limited uncertainty and that forecasts help leaders reallocate resources. However, it does not claim that a 14-day horizon is sufficient for long-term infrastructure investments or long-range staffing strategies. Those long-term planning activities typically exceed a 14-day window and are not supported by the text, so the specific inference is not derivable from the passage.

51.Option: The integration of mechanistic assumptions, such as susceptible depletion, could improve predictive performance at epidemic turning points, particularly for seasonally driven diseases like influenza and RSV.
Evidence: Our modeling suite focuses on statistical forecasts, following evidence of their strong performance in short-term forecasting tasks relative to strictly mechanistic approaches [ 21 , 22 ].

The primary model class used was a generalized additive model (GAM), which uses the semi-mechanistic assumption of a recent growth rate extrapolated forward in time [ 27 ] via the mgcv and gratia packages [ 28 , 29 ].
The COVID-19 forecasts have variation in their accuracy, with forecasts generally struggling in growth/decline phases, when the models are slow to adapt to changing trends ( Figure 4 ).
The COVID-19 Weighted Interval Score are more consistent over time than the influenza and RSV metrics, which score poorly near the peak.
51.Rationale: While the passage notes that statistical models (including a GAM with a semi-mechanistic growth-rate assumption) were chosen and that forecasts can struggle during growth/decline phases or near peaks, it does not state that integrating mechanistic assumptions like susceptible depletion would improve performance. The text contrasts statistical and strictly mechanistic approaches but provides no evidence that adding mechanistic features would yield improved predictive performance at turning points. Thus the specific claim about improvement from such mechanistic integration is not supported by the passage.

52.Option: The higher incidence of medication abortions in outer regional, remote, and very remote areas compared to major cities indicates that women in these regions are more likely to prefer medication abortion over surgical abortion.
Evidence: The incidence rate of medication abortions (9 per 1000 women) in 2020 was three times that of surgical abortions (3 per 1000 women).

Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as "abortion deserts" where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].
Previous research has shown that most women prefer one abortion method over another [ 19 ] and that abortion experiences are generally better when women receive the method of their choice [ 20 ].
Accessibility to abortion care is inconsistent throughout Australia and both geographical and financial barriers may restrict people’s choice of method [ 14 ].
52.Rationale: The passage documents a higher incidence of medication abortion in remote areas but does not provide direct evidence that this pattern reflects individual preference in those regions. It also explicitly states that surgical services are limited outside metropolitan areas and that geographical and financial barriers may restrict choice. Therefore, the observed higher incidence is equally or more plausibly explained by differences in service availability and access constraints rather than by a greater preference for medication abortion among women in those regions. The passage does not present data on stated method preferences by geographic location, so inferring preference is not supported.

52.Option: The higher incidence of medication abortions in nonmetropolitan areas is primarily due to the greater availability of telehealth services for medication abortion in those regions.
Evidence: The introduction of telehealth services for medication abortion facilitated expanded access in Australia, with the greatest benefit to rural and remote communities [ 24 ].

The incidence rate of medication abortions per 1000 women increased from 1 abortion per 1000 women aged 19–25 years in 2014 (95% CI 1, 2)—the year after mifepristone was listed on the PBS—to 6 abortions per 1000 women aged 25–31 years in 2020 (95% CI 5, 8).

Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as "abortion deserts" where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].
52.Rationale: The passage states that telehealth facilitated expanded access to medication abortion and that rural/remote communities benefited most, which makes telehealth a plausible contributing factor. However, it does not provide data or analyses demonstrating that telehealth availability is the primary cause of the higher medication abortion incidence in nonmetropolitan areas. Other factors mentioned—such as limited surgical services outside metropolitan areas, PBS listing of mifepristone in 2013, and general accessibility barriers—could also explain the pattern. Because the passage does not attribute primary causation to telehealth, this specific causal claim cannot be derived solely from the provided text.

52.Option: The strong geographical disparities in the abortion method used suggest that, for those who live in nonmetropolitan areas, there may be less opportunity to choose surgical abortion due to the limited availability of services.
Evidence: The incidence rate of medication abortions (9 per 1000 women) in 2020 was three times that of surgical abortions (3 per 1000 women).
This pattern of medication abortions being more common than surgical abortions in outer regional, remote, and very remote areas was consistently observed from 2017 to 2020.

Women who lived in outer regional/remote/very remote areas had increased odds of a medication abortion [adjusted odds ratio (AOR) 3.51 (95% CI 2.15, 5.74)] compared with women who lived in major cities.

Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as "abortion deserts" where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].
52.Rationale: The passage documents both the empirical pattern (higher medication:surgical ratio in nonmetropolitan areas and increased odds of medication abortion for women in those areas) and the contextual explanation that surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities (including 'abortion deserts'). Together these observations support the inference that people living in nonmetropolitan areas may have less opportunity to access surgical abortion, which can explain the geographical disparities in method use. This inference is consistent with the data and statements provided in the passage.

52.Option: The increasing use of medication abortion over time reflects a growing national preference for non-surgical methods among young Australian women.
Evidence: Nationally, in our sample of women who were born in 1989–95, aged 18–24 years in 2012/13, the incidence of medication abortions increased over time whereas the incidence of surgical abortions decreased over time ( Fig. 1 ).
Each incremental 1-year increase in time was associated with increased odds of having a medication abortion compared with a surgical abortion [AOR = 1.33 (95% CI 1.20, 1.48)].

Limited access to mifepristone for medication abortion has been available in Australia since 2006 through the Therapeutic Goods Administration Authorised Prescriber Scheme [ 23 ]. Wider availability only came about in 2013 once the combination regimen for early medication abortion was added to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS)...
The introduction of telehealth services for medication abortion facilitated expanded access in Australia, with the greatest benefit to rural and remote communities [ 24 ].
52.Rationale: While the passage provides clear evidence of increasing medication abortion use over time, it does not present evidence that this trend is driven by a change in personal preference among young women. The text also describes changes in availability and access (PBS listing in 2013, telehealth introduction in 2015) that likely influenced uptake. Because preference was not directly measured as the cause of the temporal increase, and because alternative explanations related to policy and access are described, concluding that the trend reflects a growing national preference is not supported by the passage alone.

52.Option: The limited availability of surgical abortion in remote areas is due to higher rates of medical contraindications to medication abortion among women in those regions.
Evidence: Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as "abortion deserts" where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].

Both methods have their advantages: for early medication abortion, these include that the process can be completed outside a medical facility, e.g. at home in privacy, and in a noninvasive manner (unless complications occur, although these represent <5% of cases).

Medication abortion through a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol is registered for use for up to 9 weeks (≤63 days) of gestation in Australia for "early medication abortion" [ 8 , 9 ]. The combination regimen can also be used "off-label" in hospitals for later-gestation abortions [ 9 , 10 ].
52.Rationale: The passage documents that surgical abortion services are limited outside metropolitan areas but provides no evidence that this limited availability is attributable to higher rates of medical contraindications to medication abortion in remote regions. On the contrary, the text emphasizes medication abortion's suitability for out-of-facility use and that complications are uncommon (<5%). There is no data presented on regional variation in contraindications or medical eligibility. Therefore the causal claim that limited surgical availability is due to higher contraindication rates is not supported by the passage.

54.Option: The increase in hospital discharge and event rates for stroke in Switzerland between 2004 and 2017 is primarily due to a rise in non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as sleep disorders and obesity, which have directly contributed to higher stroke incidence.
Evidence: the prevalence of traditional- and non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) changed, with a rise and higher exposure of non-traditional CVRF in women compared to men [ 6 ].
The overall increase in hypertension, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, and sleep disorders in Switzerland between 2007 and 2017 could have a direct impact on stroke incidence [ 6 ].
54.Rationale: The passage states that non-traditional CVRF (and increases in obesity and sleep disorders) could have a direct impact on stroke incidence, but it does not establish that these factors are the primary cause of any observed increase in hospital discharges or event rates. The language used is speculative ('could have a direct impact') and no quantitative attribution or comparison of causes is provided. Therefore the claim that the increase is 'primarily due to' those factors cannot be derived solely from the passage.

54.Option: The significant reduction in out-of-hospital case fatality from 11.0% in 2004 to 3.2% in 2017 indicates that most stroke patients in Switzerland are now receiving timely pre-hospital care, likely due to widespread public awareness campaigns and improved emergency response systems.
Evidence: The out-of-hospital CF was lower in both sexes (3.2%, CI 2.9–3.4) compared to 2004 (11.0%, CI 10.5–11.6).

Another important aspect is the population’s increased awareness of stroke symptoms and stroke knowledge [ 7 , 8 ]. Based on other stroke prevention campaigns, we expect similar trends; however, data on stroke awareness in the Swiss population are not yet available [ 9 , 10 ].
54.Rationale: While the passage documents a marked reduction in out-of-hospital case fatality between 2004 and 2017, it explicitly states that data on stroke awareness in the Swiss population are not available. The passage does not provide direct evidence that the reduction is due to timely pre-hospital care, public awareness campaigns, or improved emergency response systems. Attribution to those specific causes is speculative and not supported by the quoted text.

54.Option: The implementation of the DRG-system in 2012 led to a significant increase in stroke incidence rates in Switzerland, indicating that the healthcare system is over-diagnosing stroke to maximize reimbursement, which undermines the validity of the observed improvements in mortality and case fatality.
Evidence: We conducted a retrospective study using data from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) in Switzerland. Two different databases were used for the period 1 January to 31 December 2017: (1) Federal Hospital Discharge Statistics database (HOST) and (2) Cause of Death (CoD) statistics [ 16 , 17 ].
In 2017, all hospitalizations in Swiss hospitals were coded in the HOST database.

The discharge diagnoses (principal diagnosis or/and one of the second to fifth diagnosis position) included ICD-codes referring to an acute onset stroke like subarachnoid hemorrhage (I60), intracerebral hemorrhage (I61), other non-traumatic intracranial hemorrhage (I62), cerebral infarct (I63), and stroke non-specified as hemorrhage or infarct (I64).
54.Rationale: The passage makes no mention of a DRG-system, implementation in 2012, reimbursement incentives, or over-diagnosis related to financial incentives. The described data sources and coding (ICD-10) reflect standard administrative and diagnostic coding but do not support the claim that a DRG introduction caused increased incidence via over-diagnosis. Because the passage contains no evidence linking DRG implementation to changes in incidence or to biased diagnosis for reimbursement, this option cannot be derived from the provided text.

54.Option: The overall case fatality and mortality rates for stroke in Switzerland decreased significantly between 2004 and 2017, despite an increase in hospital discharge and event rates, suggesting that improvements in stroke care and recognition have led to better outcomes.
Evidence: stroke units were established, and telestroke networks created, resulting in lower in-hospital, 30-day, and 1-year mortality rates in those treated at certified hospitals [ 11–13 ].
The out-of-hospital CF was lower in both sexes (3.2%, CI 2.9–3.4) compared to 2004 (11.0%, CI 10.5–11.6).
The overall CF from stroke was 10.5% (women: 13.4%, CI 12.8–14.0 and men: 8.0%, CI 7.5–8.4) ( Table 3 ).
The overall age-standardized mortality rate was 33.7/100,000 (32.2/100,000 in women, 35.1/100,000 in men).
54.Rationale: The passage provides evidence that certain mortality measures have improved in specific contexts: it states that stroke units and telestroke networks have resulted in lower in-hospital and short-term mortality for patients treated in certified hospitals, and it documents a large drop in out-of-hospital case fatality compared to 2004. However, the passage does not present a direct, comprehensive comparison of overall case fatality and overall mortality rates between 2004 and 2017 (no prior overall numeric values or formal tests of change are reported). The authors also avoided P-values and hypothesis testing, focusing on descriptive trends. Because the statement asserts a significant decrease in overall rates and ties it conclusively to improved care and recognition, it goes beyond the explicit evidence in the passage and thus cannot be fully derived from it.

54.Option: The higher stroke mortality rate in women aged 85 and older compared to men is primarily due to a greater proportion of women receiving suboptimal stroke care in specialized stroke units, leading to worse outcomes.
Evidence: women older than 85 years had a higher mortality rate (715.8/100,000) compared to men (661.4/100,000) ( Table 2 ).
In Switzerland, most patients receive specialized care on stroke units or stroke centers, which are certified according to current European standards [ 14 , 15 ].
54.Rationale: The passage documents that women aged 85+ have a higher mortality rate than men in that age group, and it states that most patients in Switzerland receive care in certified stroke units. However, there is no evidence provided that a greater proportion of women receive suboptimal care in specialized stroke units, nor any data on sex differences in the quality or receipt of specialized care. The claim that the higher mortality is 'primarily due' to inferior care for older women is not supported by any quoted text and therefore cannot be inferred from the passage.

55.Option: The reduction in outpatient department visits for NCDs during the pandemic was primarily due to the reallocation of healthcare resources and personnel to COVID-19 wards, as reported in other studies.
Evidence: The management of the pandemic itself necessitated ad hoc changes to meet the surge in patient volumes, including the suspension of routine primary health services, cancellation of scheduled treatments, and the reallocation of healthcare resources and personnel to COVID-19 wards [ 7 ].
These measures led to partial or complete disruption of preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services for NCDs and other health issues [ 3 ].
lockdowns caused economic losses, making it harder for patients to pay for and use services [ 5 , 6 , 8 ], thus reducing their follow-up visits and medication adherence [ 9 ].

public fear of infection and the stigma associated with infected or suspected cases have resulted in a decrease in healthcare utilization, particularly for routine, elective, and preventive visits [ 4 , 5 ].
55.Rationale: The passage explicitly lists reallocation of resources to COVID-19 wards as one factor linked to disruption of NCD services, but it also describes multiple other contributors (lockdown measures, transport unavailability, economic losses, reduced medication adherence, public fear/stigma). The option asserts a single primary cause (reallocation) as the main reason for the reduction; the passage does not support that reallocation was the primary driver rather than one of several causes. Therefore the option overstates causality and cannot be derived solely from the passage.

55.Option: The data strongly suggest a significant impact of the lockdown on outpatient department visits for cancer and CVD, indicating that the pandemic led to a substantial and sustained reduction in access to essential healthcare services for these conditions.
Evidence: There was a 73% [RR 0.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.089–0.808] decrease in outpatient department visits for CVD and a 64% (RR 0.36, 95% CI: 0.175–0.745) decrease in outpatient department visit for cancer patients.
Among individual NCD categories, the major decline in outpatient department visits was observed for cancer (50.2%), followed by CVD (45.2%).
cancer visits were the least frequent and showed the most substantial decline, with minimal rebound.
The graph demonstrates that, after lockdown, there was a dramatic decrease in the rate of outpatient department visits by all studied NCDs, including cancer, CRD, HTN, CVD, and CKD.
55.Rationale: The passage provides statistically significant relative risks showing large immediate reductions in outpatient visits for CVD and cancer (RRs with CIs excluding 1) and describes major declines and minimal rebound for cancer. These statements support the inference that lockdown had a substantial impact on access to care for CVD and cancer. The phrasing 'sustained reduction' is supported by descriptions of minimal rebound and the observed lower post-lockdown visit levels compared with expected counts.

55.Option: The COVID-19 pandemic reduced outpatient department visits and utilization of free health services for NCDs, especially cancer and CVD, likely disrupting medication adherence and physical activity, potentially leading to complications and advanced disease stages.
Evidence: A total of 3,985,500 outpatient department visits were recorded in the 20 months before the COVID-19 pandemic compared with 2,745,395 visits during the pandemic, indicating an overall 31.1% reduction in outpatient department visits.
Similarly, the utilization of free services decreased by 12.5%, from 51,054 cases pre pandemic to 44,661 cases post pandemic.
Among individual NCD categories, the major decline in outpatient department visits was observed for cancer (50.2%), followed by CVD (45.2%) and CRD (32.6%).
lockdowns caused economic losses, making it harder for patients to pay for and use services [ 5 , 6 , 8 ], thus reducing their follow-up visits and medication adherence [ 9 ].

The consequences of limiting access to preventive and therapeutic services for NCDs—including increased mortality, poor mental health, and post-lockdown effects on chronic diseases—due to strict pandemic measures have been widely discussed in the literature [ 4 , 5 , 7 , 8 , 10 ].
55.Rationale: The passage documents reduced outpatient visits and reduced utilization of free services, and it explicitly links pandemic-related disruptions to reduced follow-up visits and medication adherence. It also notes potential adverse consequences (increased morbidity and mortality). However, the option adds an explicit claim about disrupted physical activity, which is not mentioned in the passage, and asserts progression to complications and advanced disease stages as a definite outcome rather than a possible consequence. Because the passage does not provide evidence about physical activity and only discusses potential (not demonstrated) downstream clinical outcomes, the full composite claim cannot be entirely derived from the passage.

55.Option: The lack of statistical significance in the changes for CRD, HTN, and CKD suggests that the pandemic had no meaningful impact on healthcare utilization for these conditions in Nepal.
Evidence: the model lacks adequate evidence to show the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on outpatient department visits for CRD (RR 0.89, 95% CI: 0.651–1.228), HTN (RR: 1.004, 95% CI: 0.64–1.575), and CKD (RR 0.589, 95% CI: 0.231–1.501).
This signifies that outpatient department visits for HTN, CRD, and CKD remained almost constant before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.
55.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports that the statistical model did not find adequate evidence of an effect for CRD, HTN, and CKD and interprets this as outpatient visits for these conditions remaining almost constant across the pre- and post-lockdown periods. Therefore it is reasonable, based on the passage, to infer that there was no meaningful change in utilization for these conditions during the study period.

55.Option: The observed decline in free service utilization for CVD and CKD indicates that patients in Nepal were less likely to seek care for these conditions due to financial barriers during the pandemic.
Evidence: Similarly, the utilization of free services decreased by 12.5%, from 51,054 cases pre pandemic to 44,661 cases post pandemic.
Free service utilization also declined, with the largest reductions seen in CVD (37.8%) and CKD (19.9%), while cancer services experienced a relatively smaller decrease of 6.7%.

The free health service scheme, implemented by the Nepal government, aims to provide financial relief to individuals facing severe and financially burdensome diseases such as CVD, cancer, renal failure, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, head and spinal injury, sickle cell anemia, and stroke.
lockdowns caused economic losses, making it harder for patients to pay for and use services [ 5 , 6 , 8 ], thus reducing their follow-up visits and medication adherence [ 9 ].
55.Rationale: The passage documents declines in free service utilization for CVD and CKD and describes the free health service scheme's intent to provide financial relief. It also notes that lockdown-related economic losses made it harder to pay for and use services generally. However, attributing the decline in utilization of services that are explicitly 'free' primarily to financial barriers is not directly supported by the passage; other explanations (access limitations from transport restrictions, fear of infection, reallocation of services, or logistical/infrastructure disruptions) are also described. The passage does not provide direct evidence that financial barriers were the principal reason for declines in free-service uptake, so the specific causal claim cannot be derived solely from the passage.

56.Option: The associations between household dysfunction indicators and adverse outcomes in emerging adulthood are primarily driven by shared environmental factors rather than genetic confounding.

The unique methodological feature emphasized in the paper is the use of paternal genotype as a proxy to avoid confounding from the maternal genome (quote 4) and the use of GxE with nulliparous pairs as negative controls. 61.Rationale: The passage explicitly describes stratifying on spousal parity and using nulliparous spousal pairs as negative controls to detect violations of MR assumptions (quote 1 and 2). It further states that a spurious association in nulliparous pairs can be used to quantify horizontal pleiotropy and confounding and to correct estimates in parous pairs (quote 3). This directly supports the option's claim that inclusion of nulliparous pairs enables detection of pleiotropy and subsequent correction of causal estimates.

61.Option: Unlike most traditional MR studies, our framework includes an inbuilt control for violation of core assumptions through the inclusion and comparison of causal effect estimates derived from spousal pairs who do not have children.
Evidence: Application of the MR gene-by-environment (GxE) by stratifying on spousal parity (i.e. inclusion and comparison to spousal pairs who do not have children) can provide evidence for violation of the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions and enable estimation of the causal effect of the exposure on the outcome, correcting for such violations [ 23–25 ].
Nulliparous spousal pairs effectively act as negative controls, allowing for the identification of heterogeneity in effect estimates owing to non-causal influences.
61.Rationale: The passage states that the framework applies MR GxE by stratifying on spousal parity, explicitly including and comparing spousal pairs without children, which serves as a negative control to detect violations of the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions and to correct causal estimates (quote 1). The description of nulliparous pairs as effective negative controls (quote 2) supports the option's characterization that the framework contains an inbuilt control (nulliparous comparison) for assumption violations, distinguishing it from many traditional MR designs.

62.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports a modeled PPV of 72.4% for a region with a typical malaria parasitaemia prevalence of 24%, which is approximately 70%. Because misclassified cases are non-pneumonia cases captured by the clinical definition, their substantial proportion is the direct reason the PPV is reduced to ~72% in such settings. Thus the assertion about ~70% PPV driven primarily by a substantial fraction of misclassified cases is supported by the quoted model results.

62.Option: The presence of crackles on chest auscultation and lower chest wall indrawing in malaria-positive children with pneumonia symptoms is sufficient to confirm radiological pneumonia and rule out misclassification.

62.Rationale: The passage reports statistical associations (adjusted odds ratios) between certain clinical signs (lower chest wall indrawing, crackles) and CXR-positivity among malaria-slide-positive cases, but it does not claim these signs are sufficient to 'confirm' radiological pneumonia or to 'rule out' misclassification. Associations indicate increased likelihood, not diagnostic certainty; the text also indicates small numbers (CXR-positive n=18) in this subgroup, limiting certainty. Therefore the option's claim of sufficiency is not supported by the evidence in the passage.

we estimate that, in a region with a typical malaria parasitaemia prevalence of 24% [ 17 ], 47.8% of WHO pneumonia cases are malaria-slide-negative, 24.6% are coinfected, and 27.6% are misclassified ( Figure 3 ). This corresponds to a PPV of 72.4%.
Given the assumption of 100% specificity of the WHO criteria among malaria-slide negatives, we expect all malaria-slide negatives to be in Group 1 and none in Group 0.
62.Rationale: The passage does report a 97.5% PPV among the PERCH cases under the authors' assumptions, but PPV is not the same as specificity and depends on disease prevalence. The authors also show that PPV falls to 72.4% in a region with typical malaria parasitaemia (24%), so the high PPV observed in PERCH does not imply high specificity 'in all settings.' Thus the option overstates and misinterprets the evidence.

Because the passage contains no data or analysis supporting the causal claim about the decline or its reasons, this option cannot be derived from the provided material.

Therefore the option's claim about model assumptions and explanation of a decline is not supported by the passage.

64.Option: The lack of statistical significance in the nSES association (HR: 1.35, 95% CI: 0.93, 1.96, P trend: .14) suggests that neighborhood socioeconomic status has no meaningful association with multiple myeloma incidence among Black women.

64.Rationale: The passage reports point estimates above 1.0 for nSES (HRs 1.35 and 1.28) though their confidence intervals include 1.0 and P-trend values are >0.05. The passage does not state that nSES 'has no meaningful association'; it reports elevated point estimates without statistical significance.

Evidence: Although factors underlying the differences in MM incidence by race are not fully understood, disparities do not appear to be explained by genetic ancestry [ 6 ].

Therefore the claim that the increased risk is likely due to unmeasured genetic factors is contradicted by the text and cannot be inferred from the study.

64.Option: The association between neighborhood socioeconomic context and multiple myeloma incidence is primarily driven by differences in individual-level educational attainment, as the observed risk was only significant among women with less than a high school education.
Evidence: Multivariable (MV) models were additionally adjusted for cumulative average BMI (<25, 25–29, 30–34, ≥35 kg/m 2 ), educational attainment (≤12, 13–15, ≥16 years), alcohol consumption (<1, 1–6, ≥7 drinks/week), cigarette smoking (current, past, never), physical activity (none, <5, ≥5 hours/week), and region of residence (Northeast, South, Midwest, West).

The stratified results do not consistently show the risk being 'only significant' among women with < high-school education; the reported stratified HRs vary and include non-significant estimates. Therefore the claim that the association is primarily driven by individual educational attainment is not supported by the presented results.

64.Option: Residence in disadvantaged neighborhoods has been linked to lower walkability scores and reduced physical activity, which may contribute to higher rates of obesity and, in turn, increase the risk of multiple myeloma incidence among Black women.
Evidence: Obesity [ 7 ] and pesticides (usually via occupational exposure) [ 8–11 ] are the most consistent established modifiable risk factors for MM.

64.Rationale: The passage links neighborhood disadvantage to 'obesogenic environments,' cites studies connecting lower walkability to less physical activity and higher obesity (and to MM incidence), and shows that participants in disadvantaged neighborhoods had higher obesity prevalence and lower physical activity. Given that obesity is an established modifiable risk factor for MM, the suggested causal chain (disadvantaged neighborhoods → lower walkability/reduced activity → higher obesity → increased MM risk) is a reasonable epidemiologic inference from the presented evidence.

65.Option: The improvement in timely administration of birth dose vaccines during the intervention period was primarily due to the John-Henry effect, where participants in the control period worked harder to compensate for not receiving the intervention, thereby influencing the outcome.

65.Rationale: The passage does not provide any evidence that a John-Henry effect occurred or that control participants 'worked harder' to compensate. While the trial was open-label (which can allow behavioral biases), open-label status alone is not evidence that the John-Henry effect was the primary cause of the observed improvement. The passage reports concrete outcome differences favoring the intervention but gives no data or observations about compensatory behavior in the control group. Therefore, attributing the improvement primarily to a John-Henry effect is not derivable from the passage.

Table 4 summarized the effectiveness of the intervention on the study outcomes. During the intervention period, the timeliness of OPV 0 administration (adjusted RR [aRR] 1.16, 95% CI: 1.00–1.35), BCG (aRR 1.14, 95% CI: 0.98–1.33), and OPV or BCG (aRR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.00–1.43) tended to improve compared to the control period, adjusting for other factors.

However, the stronger claim that this 'undermines the validity of the trial's conclusions about effectiveness' is not supported by the passage: the authors report statistically and clinically relevant short-term improvements and present adjusted effect estimates. Investigators considered TreeScan results to be helpful in focusing staff attention and investigation resources.

The text shows TreeScan was useful on its own for detecting and focusing investigations; it does not provide evidence that combined use with spatiotemporal cluster detection is required or that such combination is the primary condition for effectiveness. 67.Rationale: The passage states that TreeScan detected a cluster at the third allele code digit, which "encompassed a broader allele range than rule-based cluster definitions," and that this detection "alerted investigators to a local increase in Salmonella Javiana, spurring further investigation." From these statements it follows that TreeScan's sensitivity at that coarser (third-digit) level can identify increases involving a genetically broader set of isolates that rule-based definitions might not capture, enabling earlier or broader detection compared with those rule-based methods.

Evidence: We appended the allele code, which can be up to six digits, to the serotype. Whereas laboratory scientists typically compare isolates manually by using allele ranges, we used allele codes because of the standardized hierarchical nomenclature.

In the concurrent UShER version update, a subset of cases had been reassigned to BQ lineages, revealing that BQ lineages, which descended from BE.1.1.1 [ 40 ], had been present for >1 month.
67.Rationale: The passage describes using standardized hierarchical allele codes for Salmonella and notes a methodological switch (to UShER) to improve SARS-CoV-2 lineage assignment stability. However, it also documents that a UShER version update led to reassignment of cases and revealed that certain lineages had been present for over a month, i.e., reassignment contributed to delayed recognition. The passage does not claim that standardized hierarchical nomenclature necessarily ensures accurate and stable SARS-CoV-2 lineage assignments or that it reduces the risk of delayed detection. On the contrary, it highlights that lineage-assignment method changes and data updates can affect detection timing. Therefore the asserted causal conclusion is not supported by the provided text.

68.Option: The alignment between scientific interest and public attention was stronger for COVID-19 research than for non-COVID-19 research, as evidenced by higher correlations between citation metrics and Altmetrics scores.

68.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports stronger correlations between citation-based metrics and Altmetrics for COVID-19 journal articles and preprints, and provides numerical comparisons (e.g. 0.58 vs 0.33). It also states that COVID-19 papers received far greater media attention per paper. These statements directly support the inference that alignment between scientific interest (citations) and public attention (Altmetrics) was stronger for COVID-19 research than for non-COVID-19 research.

68.Option: The time-varying spikes in media attention for preprints were driven primarily by the publication of high-impact journal articles on the same topics.
Evidence: The time-varying association analysis among preprints ( Figure 5C ) revealed spikes of strong association between particular topics and media attention. For example, spikes in Topic 18 (which captures the Omicron and Delta variants) coincide with the emergence of the Delta variant (in mid-2021) and the Omicron variants (in late 2021 and early 2022) ( Figure 5C ).
The same effect is less apparent in journal articles ( Supplementary Figures S7 and S8 ), for which the strength of the topic–Altmetrics associations is less variable over the pandemic period.
68.Rationale: The passage documents time-varying spikes in preprint media attention and notes these spikes coincide with real-world events (emergence of variants). It also states that the same variable spikes are less apparent in journal articles. There is no evidence in the passage that spikes in preprint attention were driven by subsequent publication of high-impact journal articles; in fact the text suggests the preprint attention spikes are distinct and not mirrored by journal articles. Therefore the causal claim that journal publications primarily drove preprint spikes cannot be derived from the passage.

81.Option: IL-6, but not CRP, mediates the association between ACEs and LUTS in adolescence, suggesting a potential role for IL-6 trans-signalling in the biological pathway linking early-life adversity to lower urinary tract symptoms.
Evidence: There was weak evidence that the association between ACE score and any UI was mediated by IL-6 (OR NIE 1.03, 95% CI 1.00–1.06, PM 21%).

There was also weak evidence for a mediating effect of IL-6 between ACE score and daytime wetting (OR NIE 1.06, 95% CI 1.01–1.10, PM 45%), bedwetting (OR NIE 1.04, 95% CI 1.00–1.08, PM 31%), urgency (OR NIE 1.03, 95% CI 1.00–1.07, PM 19%), and frequency (OR NIE 1.04, 95% CI 1.00–1.08, PM 18%).
There was no evidence of a mediating effect of CRP (Model 2) on the associations between ACE score and LUTS (see Supplementary Table S11 ) after accounting for IL-6 as an intermediate confounder.
81.Rationale: The passage does support that IL-6, but not CRP, shows evidence of mediation between ACEs and several LUTS. However, the specific mechanistic claim invoking IL-6 trans-signalling is not mentioned or supported in the passage. The data justify implicating IL-6–related inflammatory pathways generally, but do not provide information to infer the specific signaling modality (e.g. trans‑signalling). Therefore the latter part of the option (trans-signalling) is not derivable from the presented evidence.

81.Option: The mediating effect of IL-6 on the ACE-LUTS relationship is likely due to its role in upregulating CRP synthesis via classical signaling, which in turn contributes to lower urinary tract symptoms.
Evidence: We used g-formula to decompose the indirect effects through IL-6 and CRP by using two models (see Supplementary Figure S1 ). For Model 1, we specified IL-6 as the mediator whilst omitting CRP because we hypothesized that CRP is on the causal pathway from IL-6 to LUTS; for Model 2, we specified CRP as the mediator and IL-6 as an intermediate confounder, preserving the biological pathway between the two biomarkers.

There was evidence that a higher ACE score was associated with a higher level of IL-6 (expressed as the percentage change in IL-6 per unit increase in ACE score) [1.03 (3%), 95% CI 1.01–1.05 (adjusted); Supplementary Table S8 ] but not CRP.
There was no evidence of a mediating effect of CRP (Model 2) on the associations between ACE score and LUTS (see Supplementary Table S11 ) after accounting for IL-6 as an intermediate confounder.
A one-unit increase in log IL-6 was associated with an increase in the odds of any UI, daytime wetting, and nocturia in the adjusted models ( Table 2 ).
81.Rationale: Although the investigators considered a causal pathway from IL-6 to CRP in their models, the observed data show IL-6 (but not CRP) is associated with ACEs and LUTS and that there is no evidence that CRP mediates ACE–LUTS associations. Thus the specific claim that IL-6’s mediating effect operates via upregulation of CRP which then contributes to LUTS is not supported by the results presented.

82.Option: The association between increased BMI and the risk of cardia gastric cancer is more pronounced in individuals who do not smoke or drink alcohol, suggesting that these lifestyle factors may obscure the relationship between obesity and cancer risk.
Evidence: Regarding the risk of cardia cancer, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed for non-smokers (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.29–2.85) (Q = 69.2%, P = .039).
Similarly, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed among nondrinkers (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.48–3.27) (Q = 80.8%, P = .001).
An increased risk of cardia GC associated separately with smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight/obesity was confirmed in the RERI analysis ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
However, no positive or negative additive interaction was identified for smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight or obesity ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
82.Rationale: The passage reports that the increased odds of cardia GC for overweight individuals were observed specifically among non-smokers (OR 1.92) and among nondrinkers (OR 2.20), indicating a stronger association in those subgroups. The RERI analysis confirmed that smoking, alcohol and overweight/obesity are each associated with cardia GC but did not find positive or negative additive interaction. From these facts it is epidemiologically reasonable to infer that the BMI–cardia GC association appears more pronounced in persons who do not smoke or drink, which could reflect that smoking/drinking modify the observed association (i.e., partly obscure it) when present.

82.Option: The observed higher risk of cardia gastric cancer among overweight non-smokers and nondrinkers indicates that smoking and alcohol consumption are protective against obesity-related cancer development.
Evidence: Regarding the risk of cardia cancer, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed for non-smokers (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.29–2.85) (Q = 69.2%, P = .039).
Similarly, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed among nondrinkers (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.48–3.27) (Q = 80.8%, P = .001).
An increased risk of cardia GC associated separately with smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight/obesity was confirmed in the RERI analysis ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
However, no positive or negative additive interaction was identified for smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight or obesity ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
82.Rationale: While the data show stronger BMI–cardia associations in non-smokers and nondrinkers, the passage explicitly states that smoking and alcohol-drinking status are each associated with cardia GC (RERI analysis). There is no statement that smoking or alcohol are protective; indeed they are reported as risk factors. The lack of additive interaction only indicates no evidence of positive or negative additive interaction, not that smoking/alcohol are protective. Therefore the claim that smoking and alcohol are protective is not supported by the passage.

82.Option: The dose–response relationship between BMI and cardia gastric cancer risk is independent of smoking and alcohol consumption, as shown by consistent results across all subgroups.
Evidence: The relationship between the value of BMI and cardia GC is depicted in Fig. 2 . The risk of cardia GC increases with higher BMI values, ranging from a null effect when considering the average value of the normal weight category (BMI = 21.75) as a reference to an OR of 2.06 (95% CI 1.22–3.48) for a BMI of 40 ( Table 5 ).
Regarding the risk of cardia cancer, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed for non-smokers (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.29–2.85) (Q = 69.2%, P = .039).
Similarly, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed among nondrinkers (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.48–3.27) (Q = 80.8%, P = .001).
However, no positive or negative additive interaction was identified for smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight or obesity ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
82.Rationale: Although the passage documents a dose–response between BMI and cardia GC overall (OR up to 2.06 at BMI 40), it also reports differential associations by smoking and drinking status (stronger effects in non-smokers and nondrinkers). The statement that the dose–response is independent across all subgroups is not supported because stratified results differ by smoking and alcohol status. The lack of additive interaction does not imply identical dose–response across subgroups.

82.Option: The association between BMI and cardia gastric cancer is strongest in individuals who smoke and drink alcohol, as evidenced by the higher odds ratios in these subgroups.
Evidence: Regarding the risk of cardia cancer, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed for non-smokers (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.29–2.85) (Q = 69.2%, P = .039).
Similarly, an increased odds of GC for overweight individuals was observed among nondrinkers (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.48–3.27) (Q = 80.8%, P = .001).
82.Rationale: The passage shows that the increased odds for overweight individuals were observed specifically among non-smokers and nondrinkers, indicating stronger associations in those who do not smoke or drink. There is no evidence presented that smokers or drinkers have higher odds ratios; therefore the option claiming the strongest association is in smokers/drinkers is not supported.

82.Option: The lack of a significant additive interaction between smoking and BMI, as well as between alcohol and BMI, suggests that these lifestyle factors may independently increase the risk of cardia gastric cancer without influencing the effect of obesity.
Evidence: An increased risk of cardia GC associated separately with smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight/obesity was confirmed in the RERI analysis ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
However, no positive or negative additive interaction was identified for smoking and alcohol-drinking status and overweight or obesity ( Tables 3 and 4 ).
82.Rationale: The passage states that smoking, alcohol-drinking status, and overweight/obesity are each associated with increased cardia GC risk (confirmed in RERI analysis), and explicitly reports no positive or negative additive interaction between smoking or alcohol and overweight/obesity. Epidemiologically, this supports the inference that smoking and alcohol may contribute independently to risk and do not show evidence of modifying the effect of obesity on the additive scale in this dataset.

83.Option: The implementation of the mammography screening programme in Romagna led to a temporary spike in DCIS incidence, after which rates stabilized, indicating that overdiagnosis has plateaued.
Evidence: In this way, we took into account the early excess incidence due to the introduction of the screening programme.
We also found a linear increase in incidence of 4.0% (95% CI: 1.9%; 6.1%) per year, which can be interpreted either as a trend by cohort or as a trend by calendar period.
The residual linear trend was estimated as an increase in incidence of 17.0% (95% CI: 4.9%; 30.4%) every 5-year calendar period.
83.Rationale: Although the analysis accounted for an 'early excess incidence' when screening was introduced, the passage reports ongoing linear increases in incidence (4.0% per year and a residual 17.0% per 5-year period). These findings indicate incidence did not simply spike and then stabilize; there remained a continuing upward trend beyond the initial excess attributable to screening. Therefore the claim that rates stabilized and overdiagnosis has plateaued is not supported by the reported results.

83.Option: The increase in DCIS incidence among women in northern Italy is best explained by a cohort-specific rise in exposure to environmental risk factors, particularly those affecting younger women born after 1960.
Evidence: The nonlinear cohort effect was entirely explained by the implementation of the screening programme.
We also found a linear increase in incidence of 4.0% (95% CI: 1.9%; 6.1%) per year, which can be interpreted either as a trend by cohort or as a trend by calendar period.
The residual linear trend was estimated as an increase in incidence of 17.0% (95% CI: 4.9%; 30.4%) every 5-year calendar period.
83.Rationale: The authors explicitly state that the nonlinear cohort effect was 'entirely explained by the implementation of the screening programme,' which argues against attributing the cohort pattern primarily to environmental exposures. While a residual linear trend remains, the passage does not provide evidence specifically linking that residual trend to environmental risk factors or to women born after 1960. Thus the option asserting a cohort-specific environmental cause is not derivable from the presented analysis.

83.Option: The increase in incidence rates of DCIS among screening-aged women living in northern Italy resulted from an increased detection of the disease through the screening programme and from an uptrend in the risk of diagnosis independent of the programme.
Evidence: The nonlinear cohort effect was entirely explained by the implementation of the screening programme.
We estimated a relative increase in incidence of 8.9% (95% CI: 0.0%; 19.0%) every 5-year span of exposure to screening.
We also found a linear increase in incidence of 4.0% (95% CI: 1.9%; 6.1%) per year, which can be interpreted either as a trend by cohort or as a trend by calendar period.
The residual linear trend was estimated as an increase in incidence of 17.0% (95% CI: 4.9%; 30.4%) every 5-year calendar period.
83.Rationale: The APC analysis shows that the nonlinear cohort increases were 'entirely explained by the implementation of the screening programme' and quantifies an increase associated with cumulative screening exposure (8.9% per 5-year exposure). At the same time, the authors report an ongoing linear increase (4.0% per year) and a residual linear trend (17.0% per 5-year period) after accounting for screening. These findings support the inference that both increased detection via screening and an underlying uptrend independent of screening contributed to the rise in DCIS incidence.

83.Option: The rise in DCIS incidence is entirely attributable to the expansion of the screening programme to include women aged 45–49 and 70–74, which increased the number of women undergoing mammography.
Evidence: In 2010, the target age was extended to include women aged 45–49 (annual mammography) and 70–74 (biennial mammography) years. Their enrolment was completed in 5 years (2010–14) and 2 years (2010–11), respectively.
The nonlinear cohort effect was entirely explained by the implementation of the screening programme.
We also found a linear increase in incidence of 4.0% (95% CI: 1.9%; 6.1%) per year, which can be interpreted either as a trend by cohort or as a trend by calendar period.
The residual linear trend was estimated as an increase in incidence of 17.0% (95% CI: 4.9%; 30.4%) every 5-year calendar period.
83.Rationale: While expansion of the screening programme (including ages 45–49 and 70–74) likely contributed to increased detection, the analysis identified a residual linear increase in incidence even after accounting for screening. The authors explicitly decomposed trends into screening-related effects and a remaining residual trend. Therefore it is not accurate to say the rise is entirely attributable to the programme expansion.

83.Option: The observed increase in DCIS incidence is primarily driven by the introduction of digital mammography and high-resolution ultrasound, which enhanced the sensitivity of breast imaging technologies.
Evidence: The screening programmes, indeed, may differ substantially as to uptake rate, mammography sensitivity, and rapidity and completeness of introduction of digital mammography, high-resolution ultrasound, and stereotactic breast biopsy [ 10 , 11 ].
The transition to digital mammography began during the first decade of 2000s and was completed in 2010–11 [ 21 ].
The nonlinear cohort effect was entirely explained by the implementation of the screening programme.
We estimated a relative increase in incidence of 8.9% (95% CI: 0.0%; 19.0%) every 5-year span of exposure to screening.
83.Rationale: The passage acknowledges that differences in imaging technologies (digital mammography, high-resolution ultrasound) may influence screening impact, and notes the timing of the transition to digital mammography. However, the APC analysis presented attributes nonlinear cohort effects to the screening programme and quantifies increases related to screening exposure, but does not provide direct evidence that the introduction of specific imaging technologies was the primary driver. The data do not isolate the effect of technological changes from the broader screening exposure, so the claim that imaging technology introduction is the primary driver is not supported by the presented analysis.

84.Option: The decline in the median age at multimorbidity onset is primarily due to changes in diagnostic criteria and increased healthcare utilization during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Evidence: Our findings indicate that the median age at basic multimorbidity onset decreased between 2010 and 2021, from 47 to 45 years among women and from 48 to 45 among men (see Supplementary Fig. 2 ), and similar findings were observed for complex multimorbidity.
We used primary care diagnostics and all-cause mortality information.
84.Rationale: The passage documents a decline in median age at multimorbidity onset between 2010 and 2021 and describes the data source (primary care diagnostics). However, it does not provide any evidence attributing this decline to changes in diagnostic criteria or to increased healthcare utilization during the COVID-19 pandemic. The causal explanation in the option is not stated or supported by the passage; therefore the option cannot be derived from the provided data.

84.Option: The age at onset of multimorbidity has declined over time, with younger generations reaching higher levels of multimorbidity at younger ages compared to previous generations.
Evidence: The intensity of health decline with age appeared to vary by birth cohort. Interestingly, at a given age, the multimorbidity prevalence was higher among younger cohorts for basic and complex multimorbidity, both for women and for men.

For instance, the prevalence of basic multimorbidity among women born between 1980 and 1989 was 37% when they reached the age of 31 years, but this prevalence increased to 47% among women who were born one decade later (i.e. between 1990 and 1999) when they reached the same age.

Our findings indicate that the median age at basic multimorbidity onset decreased between 2010 and 2021, from 47 to 45 years among women and from 48 to 45 among men (see Supplementary Fig. 2 ), and similar findings were observed for complex multimorbidity.
84.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports that younger cohorts have higher multimorbidity prevalence at the same ages compared with earlier cohorts and provides a concrete example (1980s vs 1990s cohorts). It also states that the median age at onset decreased between 2010 and 2021. These statements directly support the inference that age at onset has declined and younger generations are reaching higher multimorbidity levels at younger ages.

84.Option: The increasing prevalence of multimorbidity across all generations, particularly among younger cohorts, is primarily driven by rising rates of mental health disorders and overdiagnosis in the public healthcare system.
Evidence: The prevalence of basic and complex multimorbidity increased steadily during the study period for women and men—except for the older cohort, which exhibited an inverted U trend.

Younger cohorts were strongly affected by mental health disorders (with prevalence levels of 27% and 21% for women and men, respectively), which was the most-diagnosed group of diseases among this cohort after diseases of the musculoskeletal system (39% and 34%, respectively).
84.Rationale: While the passage documents an increasing prevalence of multimorbidity and notes that younger cohorts have relatively high prevalence of mental health disorders, it does not assert that rising mental health disorder rates are the primary driver of the overall multimorbidity increase. Nor does the passage present evidence of 'overdiagnosis in the public healthcare system.' Because the option posits a specific primary cause (mental health rises and overdiagnosis) that is not supported by the passage, the inference cannot be derived from the provided data.

84.Option: The socioeconomic gradient in multimorbidity prevalence and incidence is narrowing over time, particularly among younger cohorts, due to improved access to preventive healthcare services.
Evidence: The lowest-income group exhibited a higher prevalence of basic and complex multimorbidity than the middle- and, especially, the higher-income groups.

The basic multimorbidity for low-income individuals went from 60% to 78% between 2014 and 2021 among women and from 48% to 70% among men. Similar trends, but with lower levels, were observed among high-income individuals (increasing from 26% to 41% among women and from 17% to 32% among men).

The SES gradient is observed again in the multimorbidity incidence between 2014 and 2021 ( Fig. 4 ). Lower-income groups experienced higher multimorbidity incidence than their higher-income counterparts for all years between 2014 and 2021—for both basic and complex multimorbidity, and for women and men alike.
84.Rationale: The passage demonstrates a persistent socioeconomic gradient with lower-income groups showing higher prevalence and incidence and provides numeric examples showing increases across income groups. The data do not indicate that the gradient is narrowing; the provided numbers suggest the gap persists (and may even remain large). The passage also does not provide evidence attributing any change to improved access to preventive healthcare services. Therefore, the statement that the gradient is narrowing due to improved access cannot be derived from the passage.

84.Option: The S-shaped disease-accumulation trajectories observed in multimorbidity prevalence suggest that the rate of chronic disease onset slows down significantly after age 60, regardless of birth cohort or socioeconomic status.
Evidence: Overall, the disease-accumulation trajectories among the different cohorts shown in Fig. 1 were S-shaped, with fast increases at young and adult ages, slowing down at older ages.

The shape of the different multimorbidity incidence curves by age varied across cohorts: it looked to be increasing over age for younger cohorts, was inversely U-shaped for many cohorts, and was declining for the older cohorts (see Fig. 3 ).
84.Rationale: The passage reports S-shaped trajectories, noting fast increases at young and adult ages and slowing at older ages, but it does not specify an inflection at age 60 nor claim that the slowing occurs 'regardless of birth cohort or socioeconomic status.' In fact, the passage explicitly states that the shape of incidence curves varied across cohorts, indicating heterogeneity. Therefore, the strong, cohort- and SES-independent claim in the option is not supported by the passage.
